At its height, Chan Chan was the largest urban center in the Americas, home to as many as 60,000 people.

The newly discovered mausoleum is located in Chan Chan’s Utzh An complex. A staircase leads down into the tomb’s central chamber, which measures roughly 4 feet wide and 16 feet deep, according to the state-run Andina news agency. Inside this main room, archaeologists identified the remains of a single individual whose skull bore traces of a red pigment, possibly cinnabar, a crystalline form of mercury sulfide.

Some of the skeleton’s bones are missing, leading the researchers to posit that the remains were later moved or reburied. This was a common practice among Andean societies at the time, with communities continuing to interact with and even worship the bodies of their loved ones and leaders after death.

Two rooms flank the central chamber on either side. One was virtually empty, while the other held roughly 20 sets of human remains, as well as miscellaneous artifacts. Archaeologists found an additional 17 skeletons while excavating the funerary platform, bringing the total number of people buried there to at least 38.

Much about the tomb remains unknown, from the individuals’ ages and genders to the circumstances of their deaths. “What is clear to us so far is that these people were part of the elite or were associated with the elite,” Henry Luis Gayoso, an official with the Peruvian Ministry of Culture, tells the New York Times’ Alan Yuhas.

Gabriel Prieto, an anthropologist at the University of Florida who wasn’t involved in the research, tells the Times that the find is “the discovery of the decade in terms of it’s the very first time that, as archaeologists, we are able to see an elite Chimú burial.” Researchers hope that the undisturbed tomb will shed light on Chimú funerary practices and social hierarchies at a time of great upheaval.

The discovery also underscores how much of the Chimú capital remains unexplored. To date, archaeologists have excavated “no more than 7 percent of Chan Chan’s total area,” Meneses tells El País. “Evidently, the citadel has much more to tell.”
